articles.headline: OFAC Designates New Entities in Connection with Iran
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action targets entities deemed to be involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests concerning Iran.

These designations aim to further restrict the Iranian regime's access to financial resources and international networks, reinforcing the existing sanctions framework. The specific details of the designated entities and the nature of their activities were outlined in the official announcement.
This move underscores the U.S. government's continued commitment to applying pressure on Iran through economic sanctions to address its destabilizing activities in the region and its nuclear program.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organization Designations; Issues New Cuba Sanctions and Determination
body: On November 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations targeting cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations. Concurrently, OFAC also issued new sanctions specifically related to Cuba, alongside a Cuba-related determination.

These actions are part of a broader effort by the U.S. government to combat illicit financial activities, cyber threats, and to exert pressure on the Cuban regime. The designations aim to disrupt networks involved in malicious cyber activities and criminal enterprises that pose a threat to U.S. national security.
The new Cuba-related sanctions and determination further restrict transactions and interactions with specified entities and individuals, reflecting the ongoing U.S. policy towards Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-related Designations, Updates Listings, Issues Alert, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on November 4, 2026, announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. In conjunction with these actions, OFAC also published an Iran-related alert to provide guidance to the public.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. These updates reflect ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy concerning both Iran and Venezuela, aiming to refine the scope and impact of existing measures.

The amended General License for Venezuela indicates a specific adjustment to permissible activities, while the Iran-related alert serves to inform stakeholders about potential risks and compliance obligations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: On October 29, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued by OFAC to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. The issuance of an amended General License indicates a refinement or clarification of permissible activities.
This action aims to ensure that humanitarian aid and other authorized activities can continue while maintaining the overall integrity of the Iran sanctions regime.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Related to North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

These designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities that undermine international security and human rights. The actions against North Korea aim to curb its weapons proliferation programs and other destabilizing behaviors.

The designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo address concerns regarding human rights abuses, corruption, and conflict minerals, seeking to promote stability and accountability in the region.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: On October 26, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. These amendments provide updated guidance for financial institutions and other entities subject to OFAC regulations.

The updated FAQs clarify compliance obligations and best practices for handling transactions involving sanctioned parties or jurisdictions. This includes detailed instructions on when to block assets, when to reject transactions, and the proper procedures for submitting required reports to OFAC.
This revision aims to enhance clarity and consistency in compliance with U.S. sanctions programs, helping to prevent inadvertent violations and ensure effective enforcement.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran, Russia General Licenses; Removes Belarus, North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC also removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

The issuance of new General Licenses for Iran and Russia indicates specific authorizations for transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, likely aimed at facilitating certain humanitarian or other permissible activities. These actions reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions implementation.

The removal of designations for certain entities or individuals associated with Belarus and North Korea suggests a reassessment of their involvement in sanctionable activities or a change in policy, though the broader sanctions regimes against these countries remain in effect.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations on Chinese Entities for Intellectual Property Theft
body: On October 19, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations targeted five Chinese entities for alleged theft of trade secrets related to Google's AI technology.

This marks the second-ever use of PAIPA and its first application against Chinese entities, signaling a significant escalation in U.S. efforts to combat intellectual property theft by foreign actors. Associated General Licenses were also issued to facilitate certain transactions related to these designations.

China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) has rejected the allegations, stating that the progress of Chinese AI companies is a result of sustained investment in research and innovation. This action comes amidst ongoing trade tensions and increased scrutiny of Chinese technology companies.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question on October 16, 2026. This action modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela.

General Licenses are crucial tools for OFAC to manage the scope of sanctions, allowing for specific activities that align with U.S. policy objectives. The amendment reflects a targeted adjustment to the Venezuela sanctions program.
This update aims to provide clarity and potentially facilitate certain humanitarian or other authorized transactions, while maintaining the overall pressure on the Venezuelan regime.

articles.headline: China Expresses Strong Opposition to New US Sanctions on Chinese Firms Over Cuba Ties
body: China has voiced strong opposition to new sanctions imposed by the U.S. State Department on two Chinese companies, China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies Co. Ltd., on November 5, 2026. The U.S. alleges these firms supplied military-related goods to Cuba through a Cuban procurement company.

A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce stated that Beijing considers these unilateral measures a violation of international law and detrimental to the interests of Chinese companies and the stability of economic relations between the two countries. This marks the first time the U.S. has targeted Chinese companies under these specific pretexts related to Cuba.

Beijing has urged the United States to reverse its decisions and affirmed its right to take necessary measures to protect the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies. These sanctions come amidst ongoing trade and economic tensions between the U.S. and China.

articles.headline: Joshua Wong Jailed for 10 Years Over Bid to Instigate Sanctions on Beijing, Hong Kong
body: Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in jail after a High Court ruling found he partly contributed to the imposition of sanctions and adverse measures against mainland and Hong Kong officials. The court determined that Wong and fugitive ex-lawmaker Nathan Law Kwun-chung had significantly undermined national security through their actions.

Wong, 30, had previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to collude with foreign forces. The judge, Mr Justice William Tam Yiu-ho, described Wong and Law as 'advocates at the forefront colluding with foreign forces,' who exploited their connections with overseas officials to promote foreign interference.

The sentence pushes back Wong's expected release date to November 2036, as the court ordered two months and two days, representing the remaining time from a previous national security case, to run concurrently with his latest jail term.

ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula described the result as 'catastrophic' for the party, but stated that the ANC would not 'go begging for positions' during the upcoming coalition talks.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including $750 Million Penalty Against Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting significant penalties against major financial institutions. Among these, Bank of America, N.A. was assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.

This penalty against Bank of America is the largest in OCC history and comes nearly two years after the bank committed to addressing its longstanding BSA deficiencies under a December 2024 cease-and-desist order. The OCC found the bank's BSA/AML compliance program to be deficient and ineffective, leading to the failure to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions and the late filing of numerous suspicious activity reports.

Additionally, American Express National Bank was issued a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, including customer due diligence and customer identification program violations. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against two institution-affiliated parties for embezzling customer funds.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Issues Supervisory Framework for Banks' Use of 'Super Intelligence' (AI)
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued a new supervisory framework on November 4, 2026, designed to assist its bank examiners in evaluating banks' use of 'Super Intelligence' (SI), a term adopted by the Trump Administration encompassing generative and agentic AI. This framework is a significant step in addressing the rapidly expanding use of artificial intelligence in the banking industry.

The 22-page document covers various activities, including fraud detection, payments, risk management, and financial-crime compliance. While the accompanying OCC Bulletin 2026-54 clarifies that the framework does not establish new regulatory expectations, enforceable standards, or prescriptive requirements for banks, it provides crucial guidance for examiners.

The framework emphasizes a risk-based approach, where the degree of human involvement should be calibrated to the potential consequences and autonomy of the AI system. It also highlights the importance of meaningful human oversight, requiring reviewers to possess the necessary expertise, information, authority, and capacity to evaluate, reject, modify, or halt the system's actions.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Consumer Finance Monitor

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' Until January 10, 2027
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced on November 5, 2026, that it is extending the suspension of its 'End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities' rule, also known as the 'Affiliates Rule,' until January 10, 2027. This suspension was set to expire on November 9, 2026.

The Affiliates Rule, originally issued as an interim final rule effective September 29, 2025, expands export control restrictions under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to companies owned or controlled by parties on certain restricted party lists, including the Entity List and Military End-User List. It is modeled on OFAC's '50% Rule,' which prohibits dealings with companies 50% or more owned by sanctioned parties.

This extension maintains a trade truce with China, which included Beijing shelving export controls on rare earth minerals. The White House had previously announced a one-year suspension of the rule in November 2025. The decision to further delay implementation reflects ongoing U.S.-China diplomatic engagement.
articles.source: Benesch Law / Thompson Hines SmarTrade / Kharon / MLQ.ai

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, effective November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, reducing the compliance burden on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

articles.headline: DHS Adds 43 Companies to UFLPA Entity List, Largest Expansion in History
body: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), acting on behalf of the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF), announced on July 31, 2026, the addition of 43 companies to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List. This marks the largest expansion of the list in its history, bringing the total number of entities to 187.

The newly listed entities operate across various sectors, including aluminum, apparel, cotton, and tomatoes, which are designated high-priority enforcement areas by the FLETF. These companies were added based on determinations that they either source materials from the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR) or participate in government-sponsored labor transfers out of the region.

A significant portion of the additions are headquartered outside of Xinjiang, underscoring that Entity List exposure is not limited by geography and that companies elsewhere in China that source from Xinjiang or use transferred Uyghur workers are being tracked. This expansion signals a new wave of enforcement activity and increased UFLPA and forced labor enforcement risks for importers.

articles.headline: Department of War Updates Section 1260H Chinese Military Companies List
body: The Department of War (DOW) updated and expanded its list of 'Chinese military companies' (CMCs) operating directly or indirectly in the United States, in accordance with Section 1260H of the 2021 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

This list, which is required to be published in the Federal Register at least annually, includes companies that the DOW determines are involved in providing commercial services, manufacturing, producing, or exporting, and are directly or indirectly owned, controlled, or beneficially owned by, or acting as an agent of or on behalf of the People's Liberation Army or any organization under the Central Military Commission.

Notable additions to the list include technology companies like Alibaba and Baidu, biotechnology firms such as WuXi AppTec and Novogene Co. Ltd., electric vehicle and battery manufacturers, solar manufacturers, display and optical-component manufacturers, and drone and robotics companies. This action aims to highlight and counter China's Military-Civil Fusion development strategy.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
